article_text:
没後20年 井田照一展 2026年10月24日（土）–2027年1月24日（日） 豊田市美術館 展示室8 https://www.museum.toyota.aichi.jp/ 開館時間：10:00–17:30（入場は閉館30分前まで） 休館日：月（ただし、11/23、1/11は開館）、12/28–1/4 企画担当：西﨑紀衣（豊田市美術館学芸員）、成瀬美幸（豊田市美術館学芸員） 展覧会URL： https://www.museum.toyota.aichi.jp/exhibition/ida2026

豊田市美術館では、1960年代より版画家として注目を集め、油彩や水彩、立体、インスタレーションへと活動を広げた井田照一の個展「没後20年 井田照一展」を開催する。作家の没後20年を機に開催する本展では、同館が所蔵する初期から晩年までの作品約480点を通して、井田の活動をあらためて振り返る。 井田照一 （1941-2006／京都府生まれ）は、1965年に京都市立美術大学西洋画科専攻科を修了。1968年に「フランス政府留学生選抜毎日美術コンクール」で大賞を受賞してパリに留学し、その間にパリとニューヨークで個展を開催した。1960年代には独特なフォルムと鮮やかな色彩の版画で注目を集め、薄紙や紗布に図像を刷って何層も重ねる試みを経て、1970年代半ばには紙の両面に図像を刷る表現にいたる。版と紙、すなわち垂直の力と水平面が出会う場を表面とするコンセプト「Surface is the Between（表面は間である）」は、その後の幅広い作品群へと展開されていった。第11回リュブリアナ国際版画ビエンナーレでリエーカ近代美術館賞（1975）、第10回東京国際版画ビエンナーレで文部大臣賞（1976）、第8回クラクフ国際版画ビエンナーレでポーランド名誉賞（1980）、サントリー美術館大賞展大賞（1989）などを受賞し、2004年に紫綬褒章を受章した。

豊田市美術館では2004年に回顧展「井田照一 版画の思考」を開催し、版画を軸に初期作品から当時の最新作までを紹介した。本展では、多彩な版画に加え、油彩、水彩、ペーパーワーク、陶、黒陶、ブロンズ、布など、初公開作品を含むさまざまなメディアによる作品を、1966年から2006年までの同館の所蔵品から紹介する。重力によって紙の表面に窪みや穴を穿ち、ブロンズや陶の表面を圧し、あるいは内部を抉ることで新たな表面を生み出すなど、版画にとどまらない「表面」をめぐる試みをたどる。 あわせて、同館が所蔵する《Tantra》全401点を今回初めて一挙に展示する。《Tantra》は、井田が学生だった1962年から亡くなる2006年まで、変化していく自らを確認するための行為として日記のように制作を続けたミクストメディア作品で、矩形と円が描かれた同一サイズ（32.2×21.2cm）の支持体に、水彩やグワッシュ、リトグラフなどとともに、骨や石、種、綿花、涙、煙など多種多様な素材を用いている。一堂に会した膨大な《Tantra》の単体と集合により、作家の思考の立体的な紹介を試みる。

article_text:
MoreThan Films has taken international sales rights to Spanish coming-of-age drama “ Salen las lobas ” (“The Bitch Pack”) ahead of its world premiere at Spain’s Valladolid Film Festival ( Seminci ) on Oct. 25.

Marking Claudia Estrada Tarascó’s feature debut, the film is one of the anticipated discoveries in Valladolid’s Meeting Point competition. The festival’s 71st edition runs Oct. 23-31.

Related Stories

Harry Styles Waltzes His Way Through 'Coming Up Roses' Music Video

Harry Styles Closes Out 30-Night Madison Square Garden Residency With Two ‘Harryween’ Shows, Dressed as Elvis and Pizza Rat, and a Jalen Brunson Guest Appearance

Produced by Alba Sotorra (“The Return: Life After ISIS”), the Spain-Belgium-Denmark co-production follows Luna, a rebellious teenager sent to a juvenile detention center after her father accuses her of abuse.

There, she bonds with three fellow inmates. Together they dream of competing in a Barcelona trap music contest, finding friendship and a new sense of family within the institution.

The film also features in Seminci Joven, Valladolid’s youth-oriented program.

“We believe ‘Salen las lobas’ has strong potential to connect with young audiences worldwide, thanks to its universal story, the authenticity of its protagonists and its musical approach,” Sotorra told Variety .

Drawing on the real-life experience of Estrada’s sister, Valeria Estrada Tarascó, who entered a juvenile justice facility at the age of 14, the filmmaker spent four years researching the experiences of girls in juvenile detention and the legal proceedings they face.

Valeria herself plays Luna, heading a cast of largely nonprofessional performers, some with firsthand experience of similar circumstances.

“Luna found in music a way to resist during her time in detention,” Sotorra said. “All the songs in the film are original, written and performed by the protagonists themselves, who are now making their way in the music world.”

The ensemble includes rap and trap artist Marrouch Laamarti, known as Huda, Vanessa Aisha Badji and Sara Martínez, alongside established actors Rosa Boladeras (“El mal invisible”) and Alex Brendemühl (“The German Doctor”), who plays Luna’s father.

Having won Atlàntida Film Fest’s best fiction project award, “Salen las lobas” also marks the first feature under Oceanika , producer Alba Sotorra’s new banner.

The European co-production partners Oceanika with Spain’s Vampire Films, Belgium’s Novak Prod and Denmark’s Paloma Productions, whose credits include Ruben Östlund’s Palme d’Or winner “Triangle of Sadness.”

“For us, European co-production is much more than a financing tool,” Sotorra said. “It’s a way of bringing together different perspectives, talent and resources to make films that take creative risks and don’t fit conventional production models.”

Silencio Cinema will release “Salen las lobas” theatrically in Spain on Dec. 11, with indie streaming service Filmin attached and Spanish public broadcaster RTVE also on board. The film is backed by Eurimages, Creative Europe MEDIA, Spain’s ICAA and Catalonia’s ICEC.

Headed by Queralt Pons, MoreThan Films operates between Barcelona, Berlin and São Paulo, handling fiction, documentaries and experimental films for international markets.

article_text:
What can art tell us about a country where ‘excess death’ has become the fait accompli of contemporary life?

Bioscleave House (Lifespan Extending Villa) , privately commissioned in 1998 and completed in 2008 in East Hampton, is the only architectural project the late artists Arakawa and Madeline Gins realised in the US. In photographs, the four rooms of the single-family residence fan out from a central, green-ceilinged common area – the ‘meadow’, as they called it. The meadow is surrounded by undulating walls that, like the house’s exterior, have been painted in bold blocks of green, blue, red, yellow and purple. Its centre dips down to form a basin where the kitchen –the ‘campground’ – fits snugly amid a terrain as bumpy as the back of a toad, with fireman’s poles staked throughout to aid in the occupant’s climb from one area of the living space to another.

Circa 1980, following a decade of inflation and, particularly in the US, inflating healthcare costs, the artists began looking for ways to combat mortality through architecture made in service of the body. Your house can be your “physician” and your “ally”, Gins declares in a video for their Reversible Destiny Foundation. As with their handful of previous architectural projects, such as a ‘fantastical’ themepark in Yoro, Japan, and an enigmatic apartment complex in Tokyo – all designed to stimulate one’s immune system and reverse ageing through exposure to various somatic challenges – a list of ‘Directions for Use’ accompanies Bioscleave House . ‘The floor/terrain is a keyboard that is in the process of being invented,’ one directive states. ‘Try to help figure out what type of keyboard this is. Once in a while play upon this keyboard with your hands as well as your feet.’

Gins was born on Long Island in 1941 and passed away in Manhattan in 2014. Arakawa, five years her senior, had been a member of the Japanese avant-garde art collective the Neo-Dada Organizers before he moved to New York in the 1960s with, as the story goes, little besides Duchamp’s phone number and a mantra, allegedly lifted from Natsume Sōseki’s satirical novel I Am a Cat (1905–06): it went something like, ‘I’ve decided not to die.’ Over the course of their lifelong collaboration, beginning in 1963, the pair presented shows in North America, Europe and Asia with titles like Architecture Against Death (2004) and coauthored books such as Making Dying Illegal (2006); in late September, a posthumous survey of their work titled The Poetic Jump opened at the American Academy of Arts and Letters.

Bioscleave House sold for $1,250,000 upon its completion and has since been relisted multiple times. In 2023, it went for $800,000. I figured I’d be sated by a glimpse from the road, through the trees, of the broad, flat roofs on the four jutting wings. When I arrived, I saw a green industrial dumpster in the driveway. Before me, the life-extending villa stood in full view, its paint dull and peeling, wrapped in stale silence. My feet carried me forward until I saw, through the screen windows, a tableau of exposed wiring, spray-foam-encrusted ceiling beams, stripped walls and blue tape. Not even a life-extending villa is impervious to the elements and to change.

Had I gone inside before the renovations began, I can imagine that the house’s sensorial peculiarities would have boggled me the way the couple’s architectural prototype Ubiquitous Site X (1987–91/2026) did at Arts and Letters. Imagine a gigantic swim cap suspended upside-down over a platform that covers an area of about four California King beds. Once beneath it, you find the sheet of latex to be heavier than it appears. It wobbles and slaps you as you slump under its weight, onto the jagged platform (imagine crawling on a pile of Lygia Clark’s Bichos ). Your body becomes something of a caryatid – or a pea under a mattress.

In their 2002 book Architectural Body , Arakawa and Gins introduce the neologism ‘bioscleave’ as an alternative to ‘biosphere’, which for them failed to capture the dynamism of the world as they saw it. They also describe a ‘ubiquitous site’ as ‘everywhere you have landed or could land’. By ‘land’, they mean, in a literal sense, the act of registering a point of physical contact between one’s body and environment. A ‘landing site’ – a phrase Arakawa and Gins have used to title some artworks or describe others such as Stuttering God (1988–90), an installation meant to be navigated in total darkness – is defined more abstractly on their foundation’s website as ‘a kind of destination where the self is constantly reborn’.

Oddly enough, I thought of landing sites during a screening of Stanya Kahn’s short film Deny, Defend, Depose (2026) at Woodbine in mid-October. The film is a montage of social media posts celebrating Luigi Mangione’s 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, shared by users spanning the political spectrum. It opens with a few seconds of security footage: Mangione opens fire, Thompson lists and stumbles, spins around, grabs a wall for balance, but swiftly collapses, landing on the sidewalk in front of a Hilton hotel in Midtown. Today, this length of concrete looks spectacularly unmonumental. There seems to be nothing out of place save for – and these could have been present before the shooting – laminated signs by the hotel’s entrances forbidding trespassing and demonstrations. But in those seconds of security footage, the flat concrete, given a urine-yellow cast by the camera, looks radioactive with foreboding.

After the screening, members of the December 4 Legal Committee, a group formed to raise funds for Mangione’s legal defence, joined Kahn on a panel to promote their new book, Depose: Luigi Mangione, the Right to Health, and the Unfinished American Revolution (2026). Expanding on a note found in a backpack recovered in Altoona, Pennsylvania, often referred to as ‘Luigi’s Manifesto’, part of which reads, ‘A reminder: the US has the most expensive healthcare system in the world, yet we rank roughly 42nd in life expectancy’, the authors of Depose open their book by writing, ‘Every single year since 2015, the number of excess deaths in the US’ – those above the level expected in a comparably wealthy country with universal healthcare – ‘has exceeded all American military deaths in both World Wars combined… Roughly 70,000 deaths in 2023 alone are attributable to the uniquely American system of healthcare,’ one that prioritises returns to shareholders over patients’ well-being. If, as the authors argue, the bipartisan celebration of Thompson’s death is sufficient evidence of a shared sense of justice that could lead to the revolutionary reconstitution of health as common property, then that nondescript sidewalk could indeed have been the birthplace of a new political consciousness. When I brought up Mangione at an opening at Subtitled NYC, a friend responded with a story about his students debating whether the vigilante was physically attractive.

How meaningful is it today to say, ‘I’ve decided not to die’, in a country where ‘excess death’ has become the fait accompli of contemporary life? Where eccentric houses are constructed to prolong the existence of some while others struggle to afford essential medications. To be sure, it was never clear if Arakawa was completely serious in his proclamation and if he and Gins believed Bioscleave House to be literally life-extending or simply life-enriching, like any artwork. Upon further inspection, it appears that the original statement in Natsume’s novel is uttered by someone trying to fend off an insurance salesman.

article_text:
過去最大規模で、日本の女性の作家の歩みを一望する展覧会

20世紀初頭から現代まで約100年にわたる女性の作家たちの歩みをたどる展覧会 「つくる女性の100年」 が、2027年1月9日から3月22日まで、 大阪中之島美術館 で開催される。

本展では、上村松園から草間彌生、オノ・ヨーコ、片山真里まで、50名を超える作家たちの試みを、それぞれの置かれた社会状況やライフストーリーとあわせて紹介。困難に立ち向かい道を切り拓く者、家庭生活のなかから表現の糸口を見つけ出す者、自分の身体を通して社会に向き合う者など、作家ごとに一人ひとり異なる多様な芸術的実践や生き方に触れることができる。過去最大規模で、日本の女性の作家の歩みを一望する展覧会となる。

上村松園に始まり、草間彌生やオノ・ヨーコら海外で活躍した作家、具体、宮脇綾子ら

展示は時系列順にたどる全10章構成。日本画家の上村松園や洋画家の三岸節子など、女性が美術家として生きる道を切り拓いたパイオニアたちからスタートし、続いて、1920年代〜40年代の女性画家が描いた女性像に目を向ける。

1950年代〜70年代のセクションでは、海外、とくにアメリカに創作活動の可能性を求めた作家たちとして、草間彌生や、フルクサスの結成に関わったオノ・ヨーコ、そこに参加した塩見允枝子（千枝子）らの作品を展示。

続く章では、具体美術協会に参加した田中敦子や山崎つる子の活動も紹介するほか、家庭に入り家族を支える主婦像が社会的に規範となった時代背景を踏まえ、宮脇綾子らの作品を通して「手芸」を見つめる。

出光真子やイトー・ターリら70年代以降の作家、長島有里枝、片山真里まで

展示後半、1970年代〜80年代のセクションでは、「女性の立場の向上と解放を求めて」の章で出光真子、岸本清子、イトー・ターリら、「視覚と認識をめぐって」の章で辰野登恵子、寺内曜子らが紹介される。

男女雇用機会均等法の成立など、女性の社会進出が進んだ1980年代〜2000年代の章では、メディアと作家との関係にも光を当て、前本彰子や吉澤美香、90年代以降の長島有里枝らの活動を取り上げる。

さらに2000年代〜2010年代の章は「私的な宇宙と揺らぐ足元 」と題し、加藤美佳や木村友紀らの作品を展示。最終章となる2010年代〜20年代の「身体と『女性の美術家』からの解放」では、片山真里や出津京子らによる、これからの生の在り方を問いかける作品を紹介する。

この100年間に登場した女性作家たちによる多様な表現を一堂に集めた本展は、2027年注目の展覧会のひとつとなりそうだ。

article_text:
Francesco Bonami geht nach Moskau, die Art Basel bleibt nach zähen Verhandlungen in Miami Beach, und Weimer sieht mit einem rot-grün-roten Berliner Senat die Erinnerungspolitik in Gefahr: Das ist unsere Medienschau am Montag

Debatte Kulturstaatsminister Wolfram Weimer hat abermals vor einer Koalition aus SPD und Grünen mit der Linken in Berlin gewarnt . "Eine Regierung in der Hauptstadt unter Führung der direkten SED-Nachfolger würde den erinnerungspolitischen Konsens der Demokraten in doppelter Hinsicht verraten", sagte Weimer der "Bild" . Zum einen öffnet die Linkspartei nach Ansicht von Weimer dem Antisemitismus "Tür und Tor". "Gerade in Berlin, wo einst der Holocaust geplant und exekutiert worden war, darf diese Haltung nicht regieren", sagte Weimer. Zum anderen untergrabe die Linkspartei die Aufarbeitung des SED-Unrechts in der DDR. Das von Weimer geführte Kulturstaatsministerium ist unter anderem für die Förderung von Gedenkstätten zur Erinnerung an die Opfer der NS-Herrschaft und – in Zusammenarbeit mit Gedenkstätten und Institutionen – für die Erinnerung an das Unrecht in der ehemaligen DDR zuständig. Grüne und SPD in Berlin entscheiden am Montag über die Aufnahme von Koalitionsverhandlungen mit der Linken. Basis ist ein Sondierungspapier, das die drei Parteien am Wochenende vorgestellt hatten. Bei der Berlin-Wahl am 20. September war die Linke mit 25,7 Prozent stärkste Kraft geworden.

Museen

Während Russlands Beziehungen zu Europa wegen des Angriffskriegs gegen die Ukraine auf einem Tiefpunkt sind, wird Francesco Bonami künstlerischer Leiter des Moskauer GES-2 House of Culture , meldet "The Art Newspaper" . Der italienisch-amerikanische Kurator war 2003 künstlerischer Leiter der Biennale von Venedig, kuratierte die Whitney Biennial 2010 und arbeitete fast zehn Jahre am Museum of Contemporary Art in Chicago. Mit der V-A-C Foundation, die GES-2 betreibt, kooperiert er bereits seit 2010. 2024 verteidigte er gegenüber "Artnews" den kulturellen Austausch mit Russland: "Sanktionen sind wirtschaftlicher, nicht kultureller Natur. Kultur zu sanktionieren ist ein Verbrechen, das die Seelen der Menschen tötet."

Kunstmarkt

In der "New York Times" berichtet Brett Sokol, dass Miami Beach nach 18 Monaten Verhandlungen die Art Basel bis 2031 hält . Der Mutterkonzern der Messe, die MCH Group, hatte mit einem Umzug nach Las Vegas gedroht, falls die Stadt die Miete von fast einer Million Dollar nicht drastisch senke. Auf die Frage, ob die Art Basel den Standort aufgeben würde, antwortete Chef Noah Horowitz laut Sokol: "Wir müssten unsere Position in Miami Beach zwangsläufig neu bewerten." Die Stadt stimmte mit 6:1 für einen Fünfjahresvertrag mit halbierter Miete von 500.000 Dollar sowie Vetorechten gegen konkurrierende Veranstaltungen. Der Sammler Norman Braman nannte die Preisnachlässe "anstößig" und hielt die Drohung für einen Bluff: "Es ist nicht Sache der Steuerzahler, private Unternehmen zu subventionieren." Horowitz verwies auf einen "zyklischen Abschwung", wie man ihn seit den frühen 2000ern nicht gesehen habe.

Performance

Louis Lu beschreibt in "ArtAsiaPacific" Anne Imhofs Ausstellung "House of Swans" im Hongkonger Tai Kwun Contemporary als spannungsreiches Zusammenspiel von Disziplin und Freiheit, Kontrolle und Begehren. Im Zentrum steht ein vieraktiges Ballett mit Tänzerinnen und Tänzern des American Ballet Theatre und des Hong Kong Ballet. Imhof erklärt, dass die Einschränkungen des klassischen Balletts ihr paradoxerweise mehr Freiheit verschafften: "Es zwingt mich, mit seinen Begrenzungen zu arbeiten." Die Geschichte ihrer Protagonistin Amalia handele von Liebe, Macht und Selbstbestimmung. Das titelgebende "Haus" versteht Imhof, ausgehend von der Ballroom- und queeren Kultur, als Gemeinschaft und geschützten Raum für Ausdruck. Auch die Installation mit Spiegeln, Absperrgittern und Käfigen thematisiert Disziplin und Überwachung. Eine digitale Anzeigetafel, die den Countdown zum Ausstellungsende zeigt, verwandele das Museum für Imhof in eine Ruine und reflektiert die Vergänglichkeit von Kunst und Zeit.

Kunstgeschichte

Im Gespräch mit radio3 erklärt der Kunsthistoriker Wolfgang Ullrich, warum Selfies nicht einfach mit klassischen Selbstporträts gleichzusetzen sind . Während traditionelle Porträts oft dem Andenken dienen, seien Selfies vor allem Kommunikationsmittel, mit denen Menschen ihren Status vermitteln oder Erlebnisse teilen. "Ein Selfie muss prägnant sein, muss witzig sein, muss auf den ersten Blick erfassbar sein", sagt Ullrich. Durch soziale Medien entwickle sich zudem ein ausgeprägtes Gesichtsbewusstsein: Menschen wüssten heute genau, wie sie sich inszenieren. Filter und automatische Optimierungen erschwerten es, überhaupt noch ein realistisches Bild von sich selbst zu erzeugen. Zugleich erlebt die Porträtmalerei laut Ullrich eine neue Blüte, auch durch Einflüsse aus Make-up und digitaler Bildkultur. Anlass des Gesprächs ist die Ausstellung "Porträts!" in der Berliner Gemäldegalerie.

クレイフェイス

劇場公開日： 2026年10月30日

映画館を探す

予告編を見る

映画チケットを U-NEXTでお得にゲット PR

解説・あらすじ

2025年公開の「スーパーマン」および26年公開の「スーパーガール」に続くDCユニバースの映画作品で、DCコミックスの「バットマン」シリーズに登場するヴィラン「クレイフェイス」の誕生を描いた心理スリラー。美貌と名声を失った男が禁断の治療に手を伸ばし、哀しき怪物へと成り果てていく悲劇を描く。 犯罪と腐敗がはびこるゴッサム・シティ。新進ハリウッドスターのマットは事故で美しい顔を失い、世間から容赦ない嘲笑にさらされる。再起への執念から禁断の治療に手を出した彼は、傷ひとつない元の顔を取り戻すが、その副作用で身体に恐ろしい異変が起こり、心身ともに狂気に蝕まれていく。 ウェールズ出身の俳優トム・リス・ハリスが主演を務め、主人公のスターとしての輝きから、美貌を失った絶望、そして狂気の怪物へと変貌していくまでを繊細かつ大胆に体現した。共演は「ミッキー17」のナオミ・アッキー、「007 ノー・タイム・トゥ・ダイ」のデビッド・デンシック。「ウーマン・イン・ブラック 亡霊の館」「スピーク・ノー・イーブル 異常な家族」のジェームズ・ワトキンスが監督を務め、「ドクター・スリープ」のマイク・フラナガンと「ドライヴ」のホセイン・アミニが脚本を担当。製作には「スーパーマン」の監督ジェームズ・ガンや「THE BATMAN ザ・バットマン」の監督マット・リーブスが名を連ねた。

article_text:
Weekly Newsletter

Long Live Generation 6-7

Lucy Ives reviews the Krasner-Pollock show at The Met, the L train burlesque arrives in Manhattan, photos from the student protests in France, and an interview with outgoing Yaddo President Elaina Richardson.

You try to get the latest news about the inspiring student protests in France but a snarky reporter on the New York Times podcast tells you that the country’s problem is providing “too generous” pension plans and parental leaves.

These welfare benefits saddle the country with debt, he says, scolding the government for not making France more competitive in the marketplace.

You turn off the podcast because you can’t listen to any more of this evil idiocy.

You finally finish reading a much-hyped new novel and wonder why you made yourself go through such torture. You return to Marcel Proust’s In Search of Lost Time to cleanse your mind’s palette. “When one is in love one has no love left for anyone.”

You go to a gala dinner and remind yourself of the golden rule at these events: always go with the steak because you never know with chicken. You feel snazzy in your new tuxedo and remember that the last time you wore one was during the Arab Spring.

You meet with Algerian-French artist Kader Attia in a Tunisian restaurant in Manhattan for an interview about a show he’s curating in India. His face full of wisdom and passion, he encourages you to wear your wounds on your sleeve.

In the cold morning breeze, you see two doves perching on the wing of an eagle sculpture on a tall column. You think about how all good art has some connection to music, and how houses always look good when they’re painted green. Nina Simone sings “Tomorrow will be the 22nd century” in your ears. Meanwhile, generation 6-7 is remaking May 68.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

The Met’s Krasner and Pollock Show Is a Breathtaking Upending

I was married to an artist once. It was not a good experience, although calling it “an experience” makes it sound like a unified, parsable thing, and it wasn’t that, either. We’re all adults here, is what I’m getting at — so no one should imagine that anyone has bulletproof insight into anyone else’s romantic relationship, much less their own.

Certainly, once a relationship is over, it becomes a moving target in permanence: the good, the bad, and the ugly all trading places, each a microcosm in which various genres of chaos and ecstasy hold sway. And whatever we may think of other people’s marriages, we must take care. What we believe we know is almost always something we meant to say about ourselves. The phone call is coming from inside the building. If you see something, well, see something. | Lucy Ives

News

The European Parliament installs a gilded nude statue mocking Trump.

See 15 defining photos from the student protests in France .

Pope Leo says that the Catholic Church plans to renew its alliance with artists and cultural institutions amid rising threats of censorship and homogenization under AI.

NYC artists can now receive up to $10,000 in city-funded grants , double the amount of previous appropriations, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs announce.

Following contract ratifications at the Brooklyn Museum, the American Folk Art Museum, and the Guggenheim, the Whitney Museum of American Art and its union came to an 11th-hour agreement on the eve of a scheduled strike.

Francis Lee Rogers, a 63-year-old artist whose neighbors and subjects were the birds of Central Park, is found dead .

The New Museum in Manhattan will open its sixth triennial for emerging artists in its newly expanded building in February 2027.

Independent Art Fair is acquired by Informa , a London publishing, research, business intelligence, and exhibitions conglomerate.

Mary Deleary is named director of the IAIA Museum of Contemporary Native Arts, the Boston Public Art Triennial’s curatorial team, Kinosaito fall artist residents, Mariah Carey’s “Last Supper” selfie, and more in this week’s Art Movements .

Top Hollywood film and TV leaders gathered Oct. 22 for an intimate dinner and candid conversation about the future of entertainment marketing at a gathering moderated in partnership with Amazon Ads and Variety .

Executives who convened at BOA Steakhouse in West Hollywood compared notes and talked shop about the buzzy subjects that are transforming the business and execution of marketing campaigns, from tune-in to image burnishing to whisper campaigns to event promotion.

article_text:
Artículos

El abogado del mal

Javier Pérez

La película El abogado del mal es un thriller de juicio con Keanu Reeves, que es apenas un poco superior a un episodio de La ley y el orden.

Las películas que transcurren en una corte, juicio mediante, deben tener una poderosa carga dramática en las actuaciones de sus protagonistas. Además, suelen apoyarse en situaciones que ocurren fuera de la corte y que aportan mayor carga a las emociones y hacen que el espectador tome partido por alguien porque conoce elementos que los personajes no.

Pero en El abogado del mal (supongo que titulada de ese modo para emparentarla con El abogado del Diablo de 1997, protagonizada por el propio Keanu Reeves), opus número dos de Courtney Hunt, no hay elementos externos al propio juicio que aporten algo a la carga dramática. Es más: no existe tal carga en esta película que, más bien, apenas es un poco superior a un episodio de La ley y el orden , serie que Hunt dirigió hace un par de años.

El nuevo abogado de Hunt

En la película El abogado del Mal, Mike (Gabriel Basso) es un adolescente acusado de apuñalar a sangre fría a su propio padre, Boone (James Belushi), un prominente abogado que aparentemente humilla verbal y físicamente a su mujer ( la resucitada Renée Zellweger ). Tomará el caso el abogado Richard Ramsey ( Keanu Reeves ), cercano a la familia, quien tiene en contra el hecho de que el chico, aleccionado por su padre, conoce su derecho a no hablar con nadie. Sin siquiera dirigirle la palabra a su propio abogado. Así que éste deberá trabajar con lo poco que descubriendo gracias a los testigos, ayudado por la joven abogada Janelle (la desaprovechada Gugu Mbatha-Raw).

Hunt, quien tomó un guion de Nicholas Kazan (que desde 2002 no había firmado uno solo, a pesar de tener en su filmografía el de Matilda ), hace que el espectador vaya conociendo exactamente lo mismo que el abogado, con el mal tino de prácticamente ilustrar los diálogos cuando presenta los flashbacks con los que va completando la historia. La realizadora, nominada al Óscar por el guion de su ópera prima Río helado (2008), es incapaz de hacer que Reeves, un actor que no se distingue por su gran talento, cargue con la parte emotiva de esta entrega.

Lo que pensamos sobre esta película

Saturado de gestos anodinos de aparente incertidumbre, con diálogos que supuestamente nos presentan a un tipo cínico y con su clásico comportamiento acartonado (en Matrix no necesitaba mucho más, aparte de su habilidad para las machincuepas, y de Punto de quiebre ya pasaron 25 años), Reeves simplemente se deja llevar en piloto automático. La maleta que su personaje jala a todas partes, el cuarto de motel que usa como oficina para el juicio y, sobre todo, la narración en off que sitúa la historia en el pasado no son más que accesorios con los que la directora enfatiza el verdadero rol que juega el abogado en la historia y que el título en español (que se pasó por alto el The Whole Truth , la verdad completa, original) explicita groseramente.

Hunt, tal vez influenciada por su trabajo en La ley y el orden , va dirigiendo todos sus esfuerzos a que sepamos que habrá una «sorpresiva» vuelta de tuerca porque todos ocultan algo (se lo dice Richard a Janelle). Pero con los elementos arriba enumerados es fácil adivinar hacia dónde va la historia, una clase magistral sobre lo que no debe hacerse para generar suspenso. Si la premisa de Hunt fue que menos es más (economía de personajes, de locaciones y hasta de argumentos), sus desaciertos sólo sirven para dar por cierto el dicho de que la excepción confirma la regla.

Javier Pérez Nadie quiere acompañarlo al cine porque come palomitas hasta por los oídos e incluso remoja los dedos en el extraqueso de los nachos. Le emocionan las películas de Stallone y no puede guardar silencio en la sala a oscuras. Si alguien le dice algo, él simplemente replica: "stupid white man".

true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我其实非常渴望那种感觉。去做一件我从未做过的事并探索它是如何实现的，这很有趣，因为这与我平时的合作方式截然不同。但我真的很期待进入一个想象中的世界并去创造它，而不是去对已有的东西做出反应。我很享受这一次的经历，但我怀念那个阶段，并期待能在新的一年里弄清楚这一点。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我很幸运地找到了一种适合自己的工作方式，喜欢拍低成本的作品，这样我能有更多的创作控制权。因为当预算变得很高时，它就更多地关乎商业和赚钱。那样你就会失去创作自由。如果你拍出了一部成功的电影，那么你就拿到了一张想做什么就做什么的“免死金牌”，而我用我的“免死金牌”拍了《绝代艳后》。如果《迷失东京》没有成功，我是不可能拍出这部电影的。", "我太喜欢克尔斯滕了。能回到那个时刻真的很温暖，因为我和克尔斯滕很亲近，而且我看着她走到人生中的这个阶段。回想起那个时代以及我们当时是多么年轻——回想起那个时代，以及她对我的信任，还有她是如何把全部心血投入到工作中的，这感觉很美好。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "credit": "Variety · Film", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这真的让人感到欣慰，因为显而易见，我们在电影里倾注了大量的心血和工作。所以看到它现在受到赞赏并能与观众产生共鸣——我们觉得自己确实创作出了一部有价值的作品，而它当时并没有找到自己的受众。因此，它没有就这样消失，真的让人备感欣慰。", Leaving）]并将这些素材整合起来，是非常重要的事。因此，看到人们能够分享她的作品并认可她的付出，她一定会感到无比激动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本次采访经过编辑和删节。", "translated": true}]

Everything from Dunst’s performance, painting the polarizing French queen as a naive, sheltered teen seeking experience, to the film’s punk-inflected soundtrack seemed to befuddle critics."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Popular on Variety"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The film captures a propitious moment for its central figure: Sofia had catapulted forward in her career, winning an Oscar for writing “Lost in Translation” and was working with Sony, a major studio, on the visually lavish follow-up. During the COVID pandemic, Eleanor was evaluating her life and career and mentioned to Sofia wanting to do something with the footage she’d shot in France. Sofia Coppola / Courtesy of Obscured Pictures", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It was really touching to see it now because I remember her there, but at the time there was so much going on that I couldn’t really take it all in. article_text:
On the set of “Marie Antoinette,” Sofia Coppola was a director in her mid-30s with two previous features under her belt — exhilarated and occasionally overwhelmed by the scope of shooting a historical drama at Versailles. And her mother was there documenting it all.

“ Making Marie Antoinette ,” to be released in theaters Oct. 23 on Mubi, marks the 20th anniversary of the Kirsten Dunst-led biopic. And it is the product of hours upon hours of raw footage Eleanor Coppola shot depicting her daughter at work. The elder Coppola was no stranger to working this way among family: Her most renowned film may be 1991’s “Hearts of Darkness,” about the turbulent filming of her husband Francis Ford Coppola’s “Apocalypse Now.”

Related Stories

‘Big Boys Don’t Cry’ Review: Masculinity and Its Constructs Are Explored in a Revealing Docu-Fiction Study of Egyptian Bodybuilders

'Klara and the Sun' Review: There's No Life — Intelligent, Artificial or Otherwise — in Taika Waititi's Calamitous Android Fantasy

There are fewer fireworks in “Making Marie Antoinette,” which lovingly documents the work of the many craftsmen it took to conjure 18th-century France, including and especially costume designer Milena Canonero, who won her third of four Oscars for the film. The film’s existence, though, is something of a rebuttal to the initial reception “Marie Antoinette” received. Everything from Dunst’s performance, painting the polarizing French queen as a naive, sheltered teen seeking experience, to the film’s punk-inflected soundtrack seemed to befuddle critics.

Popular on Variety

The film captures a propitious moment for its central figure: Sofia had catapulted forward in her career, winning an Oscar for writing “Lost in Translation” and was working with Sony, a major studio, on the visually lavish follow-up. And it represents a coda in the career of Eleanor. During the COVID pandemic, Eleanor was evaluating her life and career and mentioned to Sofia wanting to do something with the footage she’d shot in France. After Eleanor’s 2024 death, Sofia edited together a feature out of the footage.

What emerges is a sweet tribute to Eleanor, whose observations from the time, written in her diary, are read in voice-over by Diane Lane. (Lane had starred in “Paris Can Wait,” Eleanor’s 2016 feature film directorial debut.) And it’s an opportunity to reflect on our evolving view of Sofia, who, on the “Marie Antoinette” set seemed a wunderkind and who has, with sustained creative success, grown into one of Hollywood’s most reliable indie auteurs.

Sofia spoke to Variety via Zoom about the film and her memories of shooting “Marie Antoinette” with her mom on set.

It was wild to see it on that big screen, because I was like, Oh my God, is the footage going to fall apart that big? I’d never seen it so big. But that was back where we showed “Marie Antoinette” originally, and to be back seeing this footage was a lot of emotions. But it was really fun to see it with an audience and hear people laugh and connect with it. [When editing], you’re alone with this footage, and there’s no perspective. And so I was surprised that it was fun.

The thing that was most important was showing her point of view. She really wanted this footage to be put together because she wanted to show how Milena worked, and all these incredible details of the food and the art department. She was frustrated that she shot almost 100 hours of footage that was never used for anything, which I kind of forgot. I didn’t realize there was so much footage. It was really important to show what she was interested in.

It was really touching to see it now because I remember her there, but at the time there was so much going on that I couldn’t really take it all in. It was so sweet now to see that. There’s a shot where she comes on set and rubs my back, and I was like, Oh, I didn’t appreciate at the time having a grounding mom presence in all of that craziness . I think everyone appreciated that. Everyone liked my mom because she was so calm and grounding, and to have a mom there … It was, I don’t know, sweet to revisit a lot of that time and to see Jason [Schwartzman] because he’s always sweet and funny.

But it made me appreciate her. She loved to visit set, and she was there for such a span of time — like part of the team.

Yeah, I left that in because … I thought, OK, who cares? Nobody cares. I have a cold. Why are we putting this in the movie? It felt indulgent, a little bit, but then I thought, it’s such a unique thing that it’s my mom, who’s also being a mom while she’s being a documentarian. So I thought it was sweet.

Me being cranky.

I’m glad, because it was embarrassing. It’s embarrassing to show me being irritated with my mom — I was like, “Do we have to leave this in?” But it’s in the spirit of my mom, who loves to show the real side of things and I think it’s such a universal thing.

We just grew up, luckily, around creativity and having that encouraged. My mom encouraged us so much, and now seeing it as a mother of a young artist, I have a whole other perspective of appreciating that and the way she’s seeing what I’m making, the same way I love seeing what my daughter’s making and I’m so proud of that.

I try to encourage my kids, and my mom was never like “I want them to do things my way.” I love seeing how they do things their way and discovering what they’re into, and she was very encouraging in that way. It was always fun as a little kid to make drawings, which she would be delighted by in the same way she was on the set. I share that: Of course it’s so thrilling to have kids that are creative when you’re seeing what they’ve made.

No, it was sort of a tradition — [filming] was one of her skills. She contributed that on sets, and she filmed on a lot of my dad’s sets and she was on “The Virgin Suicides” and “Lost in Translation.” I wonder if she was on all of my sets. Maybe not all of them, but she would come, because you always need BTS footage for when they’re promoting it. So it was just sort of like something that she could offer. There was a DVD supplement for “Virgin Suicides” that she filmed. But this was the most in-depth. We didn’t realize that she had almost 100 hours of footage until she brought it up and wanted to revisit it.

Maybe. I don’t know. After [”Marie Antoinette”], I was like, Oh, yeah, I just want to be with two actors in a hotel — like a reaction. [Coppola’s follow-up film, 2010’s “Somewhere,” shot at the Chateau Marmont in Los Angeles.]

At one point, I was looking at Edith Wharton’s “Custom of the Country,” and I was excited about doing a period costume piece again, because I love seeing it all come together. But nothing on that scale, with all the extras. I don’t know. That was so massive. I was a little lost in all the coordination of so many people. But we probably do it differently now.

Now, when I see the opera scene and we’re talking about changing the costumes, the wigs — now that I’m experienced, I’m like, Nobody would notice. Just move the people around a little — you don’t have to change all their wigs. But you don’t know that until you make stuff.

Now it’s changed, because there’s a lot more women department heads and in the crew and it’s not so unusual to think about a female perspective. I hope that, for young filmmakers, it’s helpful to see someone on set, a woman working with a lot of guys, seeing someone sticking to what they have in mind and making it happen — I hope that’s helpful.

I’m actually really craving that. It was fun to do something I had never done and discover how that comes about, because it’s so different from how I usually work. But I’m really looking forward to going into an imaginary world and creating that, as opposed to kind of reacting to what you have. I’ve enjoyed this, but I miss that stage and I’m looking forward to trying to figure that out in the new year.

I luckily found a way to work where I like to do things lower-budget, so I have more creative control. Because when they get to be big budgets, it’s more about the business and having to make money. Then you lose creative freedom. If you make a successful film, then you have a free pass to do whatever you want, kind of, and I used my free pass to do “Marie Antoinette.” I wouldn’t have been able to make that if “Lost in Translation” hadn’t been successful.

It’s always challenging, especially now, to make a film, but luckily I have a body of work and I keep the budget small enough where I’ve been able to keep making them. But we’ll see.

I love Kirsten so much. It was sweet to go back to that moment because I’m close to Kirsten, and I see her at this stage of her life. And it was sweet to remember that time and how young we both were — remembering that time and the trust she has in me, and how she really puts her heart into her work.

I loved her performance, and the critics gave her a hard time when it came out. She felt bad, because she was carrying the movie. I’m glad that people appreciate her performance. It’s just sweet to see her at that stage and remember that time we spent.

It’s just really gratifying, because obviously we put a lot of work and heart into the movie. So to see it being appreciated and connecting with the audience now — we felt like we made something worthwhile, and it didn’t find its audience. So it’s just been gratifying that it didn’t just disappear.

It was completing her work that she wanted to have done. She had a real vision of this footage. It was never intended to be a film, but then she needed this to be put together and there was enough. It was really important at the end of her life that her book was published [the 2025 memoir “Two of Me: Notes on Living and Leaving”] and that this was put together. And so she would be so thrilled that people get to share her work and appreciate her for her work.

article_text:
Source: parliament.tv

Pete Johnson, Claire Mundell, Harriet Finney

The UK production community is “very concerned” about what impact the proposed US federal tax incentive will mean for the UK industry, as stressed during a Culture, Media and Sport (CMS) Committee hearing in UK parliament yesterday (November 11).

Glasgow-based Claire Mundell, managing director of Synchronicity Films, was speaking in front of the cross-party committee alongside BFI deputy CEO Harriet Finney and British Screen Forum chief executive Pete Johnson, as a follow-up to the committee’s inquiry into British film and high-end TV, which ran from 2023-25.

“In the production community we are very concerned about the proposed US incentives that are on the horizon and what they will do to inward investment in the UK,” said Mundell, stressing the income producers receive from working on a service basis for these projects to help fund their own companies, as well as the skills and training opportunities they provide. Synchronicity’s credits include Sky series The Tattooist Of Auschwitz.

These concerns have been intensified by a slowdown in inward investment in the UK, as revealed in stats published on November 10 by the BFI highlighting inward investment spend on film in the UK was down 40% in the first nine months of 2026, compared to 2025.

“We are seeing a global reduction in commissioning. Hollywood is commissioning less around film and HETV,” said Finney. “The key thing is the UK’s market share remains robust and high, but we do need to think about the competitive environment that is around us.

“We are definitely seeing other territories who look to the UK as an absolute model of how the production landscape can be shaped around skills, around workforce, around talent, and importantly around the tax incentives as well. Ireland, our neighbouring territories in Europe, Australia, definitively are much more competitive environments, as we look ahead also to the US federal tax incentive.”

“The trick we need to pull off is to retain and build that inward investment – we don’t want to lose any of that,” said Johnson. “But also, to recognise we need a stronger domestic economy.”

Across the whole of 2025, 91% production in UK inward investment and only 7% was UK production. In the first nine months of 2026, the BFI’s stats also showed that spend on local UK features in Q1-3 2026 was down by 17%.

To help bolster local UK production, Johnson advocated for an extension of the research and development (R&D) tax relief to film. It is currently limited to companies investing in scientific or technological innovation. He believes it would have “a significant impact” and noted other countries already allow their creative companies to claim R&D relief.

Finney said a report on what the impact of the introduction of the Independent Film Tax Credit (IFTC) in 2024 will be published next year.

Mundell added, “Very specific British cultural stories are the hardest to fund at the moment” via the market, and in particular, “anything with a regional accent become very dependent on low budgets”.

Problems around support for the distribution of UK film was also acknowledged. A BFI box office report published on November 10 revealed that from January to September of this year, the market share of UK qualifying independent films at the box office was 6.8%, compared with 7.5% for the same period last year

“UK films are not cutting through at box office,” said Finney, with chair of the committee, Conservative MP Caroline Dinenage, noting recent disappointment in the industry that a prints and advertising tax relief to help with distribution costs for independent film was not introduced in the autumn budget, as had been expected.

UK government “open-minded” about AgoraEU

In the second part of the committee session, creative industries minister Ian Murray was asked about whether the UK would consider joining the media strand of AgoraEU. The CMS committee’s inquiry into British and high-end TV film published a list of recommendations to the government for the sector in 2025, of which rejoining AgoraEU predecessor Creative Europe post-Brexit was one.

“They don’t know what the final structure of that will look like, or what the cost will be,” said Murray of the new-look AgoraEU.

Pushed by Dinenage on whether the UK has completely ruled out joining, Murray said, “We have at this stage – but we are open minded to see what it looks like.”

He also left the door slightly ajar to a UK streamer levy, something both the last Conservative government, and the current Labour government, have repeatedly shied away from.

“We did rule out a streamer levy… we don’t believe at this stage that mechanism is needed, because you can see significant investment coming into the country with all of that matrix of funding,” said Murray. “It’s been ruled out at this stage – but given the way in which the market is going, given that fragility, we’re always looking at whether or not the tax relief system and the environment is conducive, and we will continue to do so.”

Dinenage also pressed Murray on how front-footed he has been in advocating for the sector with Treasury, on issues such as tax incentives. When asked how many times he has met with his equivalent minister in the Treasury department – having taken on this role in September 2025 – Murray said he had done so just once, before the summer.

“Not good enough,” responded Dinenage.

National Lottery assurances

Murray did give some positive assurances about National Lottery funding. A review into how the National Lottery allocates its funding is currently underway. National Lottery ‘good cause’ funding makes up around a third of the BFI’s budget.

“The National Lottery review will not affect people’s funding as it sits at the moment,” said Murray. “This is a review of what will happen with additional future funding. The core money that goes to the BFI will not fall as a result of the work we are doing with the National Lottery review.”

“Us working better with other lottery distributors is really a key as part of that,” said Finney, of how the BFI can make the lottery money work harder. “Us working better in local communities, with local decision makers, is really important.

“The one thing I would say, in terms of the share – we have 2.7% of the share, that’s £50m. Only 10% of the applications we receive can we meet. In some of the programmes, it’s only 3%.”
